title: Baldwin beats Maui High 48–31 in MIL Division I football
excerpt: The Bears won their third meeting of the season with the Sabers, 48–31 on Friday night at King Kekaulike, and kept a seven-game win streak alive.
body:
The Bears won their third meeting of the season with the Sabers, 48–31 on Friday night at King Kekaulike, and kept a seven-game win streak alive.

Baldwin beat Maui High 48–31 in Maui Interscholastic League Division I football on Friday night, Oct. 23, at King Kekaulike, according to KHON2 and MaxPreps.

Third win over the Sabers this fall

It was the third Baldwin–Maui High meeting of the 2026 season, and the Bears won all three. Baldwin blanked Maui High 36–0 on Aug. 29, according to The Maui News and MaxPreps, then won again 20–7 on Oct. 3, The Maui News reported. Across those three games, Baldwin scored 104 points to Maui High’s 38.

What the result means

Baldwin had already locked up the MIL Division I title and a state tournament berth with its 13–3 win at Lahainaluna on Oct. 16, according to The Maui News. MaxPreps lists the Bears on a seven-game winning streak after Friday’s win.

The game was played at King Kekaulike as a neutral-site contest on the MIL Division I schedule.

Up next

Maui High visits Lahainaluna on Friday, Oct. 30, at 7 p.m. Baldwin’s next listed game is against Lahainaluna on Saturday, Nov. 7, at a site the MIL hasn’t named yet. See every remaining game and result in our MIL Football Schedule 2026 guide.

title: Uptempo Maui Halloween basketball clinic for ages 4–8 set for Oct. 27 in Wailuku
excerpt: Uptempo Athletics Maui is hosting a one-day pop-up clinic for young and beginning players on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at Puʻu Kukui Elementary School.
body:
Uptempo Athletics Maui is hosting a one-day pop-up clinic for young and beginning players on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at Puʻu Kukui Elementary School.

Got a little one who loves to dribble? Uptempo Athletics Maui has a Halloween pop-up basketball clinic on the calendar for keiki ages 4 to 8, and it’s open to brand-new players as well as kids who already love the game.

Clinic details

  • When: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 4:45 to 5:30 p.m.
  • Where: Puʻu Kukui Elementary School, Wailuku
  • Ages: 4 to 8. The sign-up form has a group for 4- and 5-year-olds and a group for 6- to 8-year-olds, both in the same time slot.
  • Cost: $30, paid when you register on the clinic registration form. Uptempo says fees are non-refundable.
  • Bring: a basketball, a water bottle, comfortable athletic clothes, and basketball or running shoes.

The clinic focuses on basics like dribbling, shooting and movement, with games mixed in. Uptempo says it will email a reminder with more details to registered families shortly before the clinic, so check your junk folder if it doesn’t show up. The schedule may change, so watch for that email.

Where Uptempo is playing these days

Uptempo’s previous lease ended, and the program is looking for a new permanent gym, according to its FAQ page. In the meantime, leagues, classes, clinics and private training continue at partner sites such as Puʻu Kukui Elementary and Old Wailuku Gym. Locations vary by program and are shared at registration.

Also coming up

Registration is open for Uptempo’s youth league, with kindergarten through 5th grade divisions and a girls division for ages 6 to 8. The season starts in November, according to the registration page.

Find more programs like this in our Uptempo Athletics Maui directory listing and on our basketball page. Running a keiki clinic or camp? Tell us about it.

title: King Kekaulike wins the MIL Division I girls volleyball title
excerpt: The Nā Aliʻi lost the first set, then took the next three to beat defending champion Kamehameha Maui 3–1 at the Warriors’ gym.
body:
The Nā Aliʻi lost the first set, then took the next three to beat defending champion Kamehameha Maui 3–1 at the Warriors’ gym.

King Kekaulike is the 2026 MIL Division I girls volleyball champion. The Nā Aliʻi beat Kamehameha Maui 3–1 on Tuesday night, Oct. 20, at the Warriors’ Kaʻulaheanuiokamoku Gymnasium, according to MaxPreps.

A year of waiting

The win flips last season’s ending. Kamehameha Maui beat King Kekaulike in five sets for the 2025 league title, according to The Maui News, and came into this season as the defending champion.

A slow start, then three straight sets

Kamehameha Maui won the opening set 25–20. King Kekaulike answered by winning the second set 25–21, took the third, and closed it out 25–21 in the fourth, based on the set-by-set updates posted by Kamehameha Maui athletics. The third-set score wasn’t included in those updates.

It was King Kekaulike’s second win over the Warriors in eight days, after a 3–1 win in their regular-season meeting on Oct. 13. The MaxPreps schedule now shows a seven-match winning streak for the Nā Aliʻi.

How they got here

King Kekaulike swept Lahainaluna 3–0 in Monday’s semifinal, and Kamehameha Maui swept Maui High 3–0 in the other. Lahainaluna had reached the semifinals by beating Baldwin in Saturday’s play-in. Catch up on the first rounds of the playoffs.

Up next: Division II playoffs at Maui Prep

The Division II girls volleyball playoffs run Wednesday through Friday, Oct. 21–23, at Maui Prep, with the final set for Friday at 6 p.m., according to the MIL schedule. If you’re heading out, check with the schools for any last-minute changes.

Congratulations to both teams on a great season, and good luck to everyone still playing. Have a score we missed? Send it to us.

title: Catching up: Molokaʻi edges Hāna for the MIL eight-player football title
excerpt: The Farmers beat Hāna 24–19 on Oct. 17 to clinch the league championship, a month after a 14–13 win over the Dragons at Hāna.
body:
The Farmers beat Hāna 24–19 on Oct. 17 to clinch the league championship, a month after a 14–13 win over the Dragons at Hāna.

Molokaʻi is the 2026 MIL eight-player football champion. The Farmers wrapped up the title with a 24–19 win over Hāna on Saturday, Oct. 17, according to The Maui News.

An early cushion, then one more answer

Molokaʻi scored all 18 of its first-half points in the opening quarter. Hāna kept coming, putting up 19 unanswered points and moving in front 19–18 early in the fourth quarter. Molokaʻi went back ahead on a touchdown pass with about seven minutes to play, and the defense made the five-point lead stand.

Two close wins over the Dragons

The title game was the second tight finish between these two teams this fall. Molokaʻi also won 14–13 on Sept. 18 at Hāna, a game listed on the MIL eight-player schedule. The Farmers finished 3–1 in league play, The Maui News reported.

Hāna had a strong stretch of its own, beating Lānaʻi 20–0 on Oct. 2 and 36–20 on Oct. 10. Catch up on Hāna’s fourth-quarter shutout and its win on Lānaʻi.

Up next in MIL football

Eleven-player MIL football keeps going tonight, Friday, Oct. 23, with Baldwin and Maui High at 7 p.m. at King Kekaulike, and Kamehameha Maui hosts Kūlanihākoʻi on Saturday at 6 p.m. See every remaining game and result in our MIL Football Schedule 2026 guide.

Congratulations to the Farmers on the championship, and to the Dragons on a hard-fought season. Have a score we missed? Send it to us.

body:
Every remaining Maui Interscholastic League football game, the results so far, and the dates for the HHSAA state tournament in one place.

Last updated Oct. 24, 2026

This MIL Football Schedule 2026 guide covers the rest of the Maui Interscholastic League regular season, the results we’ve confirmed so far, and what comes next at the state tournament. Dates, sites and kickoff times come from the official MIL Division I football schedule, and we’ll keep this page updated as games are played.

How MIL football is set up in 2026

The MIL plays one 11-player varsity schedule with six schools: Baldwin, Kamehameha Maui, King Kekaulike, Kūlanihākoʻi, Lahainaluna and Maui High. The league posts it as Division I football. Hāna, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi play a separate eight-player schedule. The MIL doesn’t post a separate Division II football schedule, but the HHSAA gives the league one Division I spot and one Division II spot at the state tournament.

The MIL Division I girls volleyball playoffs got going on Saturday, Oct. 17, and by Monday night the field was down to two: Kamehameha Maui and King Kekaulike.

Lahainaluna opened the playoffs with a 3–1 win over Baldwin at Lahainaluna High School Gym (25–20, 25–22, 15–25, 25–20). Baldwin took the third set and kept the other three close, according to the MaxPreps recap.

Two sweeps in the semifinals

Both semifinals were played Monday, Oct. 19, at Kamehameha Maui’s Kaʻulaheanuiokamoku Gymnasium. King Kekaulike moved on with a 3–0 win over Lahainaluna, and MaxPreps reports it was the Nā Aliʻi’s sixth straight win.

In the night match, Kamehameha Maui swept Maui High 3–0 (25–19, 25–21, 25–19), according to the Kamehameha Maui athletics schedule.

title: Fueling keiki athletes: a parent’s guide to food and drinks for youth sports
excerpt: What the research says about everyday meals, game-day food, water versus sports and energy drinks, supplements, and why eating enough matters for young athletes on Maui.
body:
What the research says about everyday meals, game-day food, water versus sports and energy drinks, supplements, and why eating enough matters for young athletes on Maui.

General information, not medical advice. Every keiki is different. Talk with your child’s doctor, athletic trainer or a registered dietitian before making changes, especially if your child has a health condition, food allergy or special diet.

No games to report today, so we’re looking at something that matters every day of the season: what our keiki eat and drink. Between after-school practice, weekend tournaments and Maui’s heat, young athletes need steady fuel. Here’s what the major medical and sports-health groups say.

Start with everyday meals

Good sports nutrition isn’t really about one special pregame meal. A joint position paper from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine says performance and recovery both improve with well-chosen nutrition, meaning the right type, amount and timing of food and fluids. In practice that means regular meals and snacks with a mix of carbohydrates, protein, fruits and vegetables, built around the family’s normal food. Rice, poi, ʻulu, sweet potato, fish, chicken, eggs, tofu and local fruit all fit.

The same paper recommends that athletes who want a personal plan see a registered dietitian. That’s a good option for teens in heavy training or anyone with specific concerns.

Eating enough is a safety issue

The most common problem in youth sports isn’t eating the “wrong” food. It’s not eating enough for how much a child trains. The International Olympic Committee’s 2023 consensus statement describes Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs): health and performance problems that happen in both girls and boys when food intake doesn’t keep up with exercise. The statement also points to links between REDs and mental health.

For parents and coaches, that means avoiding pressure about weight or body size, and paying attention if a young athlete is skipping meals, constantly tired, getting hurt often or losing interest in a sport they love. Those are reasons to check in with a doctor.

Water first

For most practices and games, water is the go-to drink. The American Academy of Pediatrics warns that sports drinks and energy drinks are often marketed to kids for the wrong reasons. It says the caffeine and other stimulants in energy drinks have no place in the diet of children and teens, and that drinking sugary sports drinks often or in large amounts can raise the risk of overweight and obesity.

The AAP report treats sports drinks and energy drinks as very different products. Sports drinks may have a role for athletes in long or high-intensity activity, but that’s a question for your child’s doctor or athletic trainer. Energy drinks don’t belong in the cooler.

Hydration in Maui heat

The National Athletic Trainers’ Association says athletes need easy access to water to avoid becoming dehydrated, but it also warns that drinking far too much can be harmful. Its advice is to plan fluids before, during and after activity that are enough but not excessive, and it notes that habits improve when water is easy to get and kids know why it matters.

Heat is a separate risk. NATA’s position statement on exertional heat illnesses calls exertional heat stroke one of the leading causes of sudden death in sport and urges teams to have an emergency plan at every venue. Practical steps for families: send a full, labeled water bottle to every practice, ask coaches about water breaks and shade, and know that hydration is only one part of staying safe in the heat.

Supplements: usually not needed

Protein powders, pre-workout mixes and other products are easy to find online. The AAP reviewed performance-enhancing substances in young athletes and raised concerns about high rates of product contamination and a link with later steroid use. It also found that for most young athletes, these products don’t add meaningful gains beyond the natural growth of puberty plus good food and training.

A simple checklist for families

  • Three meals a day plus snacks on training days. Don’t skip breakfast before school and afternoon practice.
  • Pack a snack for the drive home after practice. Long days on Maui roads add up.
  • Water bottle every day. Skip energy drinks entirely.
  • Check with a doctor or registered dietitian before buying supplements.
  • Watch for tiredness, frequent injuries or worry about weight, and speak up early.

Coaches, athletic trainers or dietitians on Maui with tips for keiki athletes? Send them to us and we may feature them in a future story.

Sources:

Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and American College of Sports Medicine, “Nutrition and Athletic Performance” (2016)

American Academy of Pediatrics, “Sports Drinks and Energy Drinks for Children and Adolescents: Are They Appropriate?” (2011)

American Academy of Pediatrics, “Use of Performance-Enhancing Substances” (2016)

National Athletic Trainers’ Association, “Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active” (2017)

National Athletic Trainers’ Association, “Exertional Heat Illnesses” (2015)

International Olympic Committee consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), British Journal of Sports Medicine (2023)

This article is general information, not medical advice. Talk with a health professional about your child’s needs.

title: Catching up: Hāna scores 20 in the fourth to shut out Lānaʻi
excerpt: Hāna and Lānaʻi were scoreless through three quarters before the Dragons scored 20 straight in the fourth for a 20–0 eight-player football win on Oct. 2.
body:
Hāna and Lānaʻi were scoreless through three quarters before the Dragons scored 20 straight in the fourth for a 20–0 eight-player football win on Oct. 2.

One more early-October result for the record books, and it was a nail-biter until the very end.

Hāna hosted Lānaʻi in an eight-player MIL football game on Friday, Oct. 2, and neither team could find the end zone for three full quarters. Then the Dragons’ defense broke it open. An interception returned for a touchdown, plus a two-point conversion, gave Hāna an 8–0 lead. A second defensive score, this time on a fumble recovery, made it 14–0 after the two-point try came up short. A 6-yard touchdown run finished off the 20–0 shutout, according to The Maui News.

The two teams met again eight days later on Lānaʻi, and Hāna won that one too, 36–20. Read our recap of the rematch.

title: Weekend roundup: Kamehameha Maui tops King Kekaulike, Baldwin wins at Lahainaluna
excerpt: In football, Kamehameha Maui beat King Kekaulike 27–14 and Baldwin won at Lahainaluna 13–3; in girls volleyball, Seabury Hall and Hāna won Friday night.
body:
In football, Kamehameha Maui beat King Kekaulike 27–14 and Baldwin won at Lahainaluna 13–3; in girls volleyball, Seabury Hall and Hāna won Friday night.

In football, Kamehameha Maui won the big Saturday night game, beating King Kekaulike 27–14 on the Nā Aliʻi’s home field on Oct. 17. KHON2 had called it a big MIL showdown. It was the Warriors’ second win over King Kekaulike this season, after a 31–7 football win on Sept. 18.

On Friday, Oct. 16, Baldwin won a low-scoring football game at Lahainaluna, 13–3. MaxPreps reports it was the Bears’ sixth straight win and their second over the Lunas this season, after a 27–19 football win on Sept. 18. Next up, according to MaxPreps, Baldwin visits Maui High this Friday night, and Lahainaluna hosts Maui High on Oct. 30.

In MIL Division II girls volleyball on Friday night, Seabury Hall swept Kūlanihākoʻi 3–0 (25–13, 25–16, 25–8) at home in Makawao. Hāna beat Lānaʻi 3–1 (25–19, 25–17, 24–26, 25–15) at Hāna School Gym, with Lānaʻi taking a tight third set 26–24, according to ProspectsHI’s HSVB Hub.

Hāna and Lānaʻi met again on Saturday morning in Hāna. We’re still confirming that score and will add it once it checks out.

Hāna beat Lānaʻi 36–20 in eight-player football, and King Kekaulike swept Baldwin 3–0 during a seven-match girls volleyball win streak.

On Saturday, Oct. 10, Hāna beat Lānaʻi 36–20 in an eight-player MIL football game on Lānaʻi. Lānaʻi grabbed a brief 8–6 lead on a long punt return, but Hāna led 12–8 at halftime and outscored the Pine Lads 24–12 after the break. The Dragons have now won two straight to improve to 2–1, while Lānaʻi fell to 1–3, according to The Maui News.

In MIL Division I girls volleyball, King Kekaulike swept Baldwin 3–0 at Baldwin High School Gym on Thursday, Oct. 8. It was one piece of a big run: after sweeping Kamehameha Maui on Oct. 13, King Kekaulike has won seven straight and stands 8–2 in league play, according to ProspectsHI’s HSVB Hub.

body:
King Kekaulike beat Lahainaluna and Kamehameha Maui, Baldwin and Maui High each won a five-set match, and Seabury Hall improved to 10–0 in MIL Division II.

King Kekaulike had a big stretch in MIL Division I girls volleyball. It beat Lahainaluna 3–0 (25–20, 25–20, 25–21) at home on Tuesday, Oct. 6, then beat Kamehameha Maui 3–1 (10–25, 25–22, 25–17, 27–25) on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

Also on Oct. 6, Kamehameha Maui won 3–1 at Baldwin (27–25, 22–25, 26–24, 25–15). On Thursday, Oct. 8, Maui High dropped the first two sets to Lahainaluna, then came back to win 3–2 (17–25, 22–25, 25–15, 25–16, 15–10). Maui High went five again on Oct. 13, and this time Baldwin won it at home, 3–2 (22–25, 25–15, 11–25, 25–16, 15–8).

In Division II, Seabury Hall swept Maui Prep 3–0 (25–16, 25–16, 25–19) at home on Wednesday, Oct. 14. That’s 10 straight wins and a 10–0 league record for the Spartans, who host Kūlanihākoʻi on Friday, Oct. 16, at 6 p.m.

body:
Maui Sports Leagues lists late registration through Oct. 24 at $140, with the fall season scheduled to begin Oct. 17.

Regular pricing ended Sept. 30. Maui Sports Leagues’ published late-registration window runs Oct. 1–24 at $140.

The season is scheduled Oct. 17–Dec. 12, with coed 4U–14U and girls 8U–16U divisions. Families must obtain a team coach’s approval before registering; the league states that payments are nonrefundable. Contact the league about openings and team placement.

title: Free Surf-N-Turf youth program heads into final September session
excerpt: Mana O Maui’s free Surf-N-Turf afterschool program is scheduled to hold the final session of its September series on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
body:
Mana O Maui’s free Surf-N-Turf afterschool program is scheduled to hold the final session of its September series on Wednesday, Sept. 30.

The program serves Maui youth ages 11 to 17 and combines surfing or hiking depending on conditions. The September series was scheduled for four Wednesdays, with transportation offered from Central Maui pickup points.

The program is designed to get young people outdoors after school while providing structured recreation and access to Maui’s natural environment.

title: Menehune Basketball League continues through December
excerpt: The County of Maui’s 2026 Menehune Basketball League is underway, giving sixth-, seventh- and eighth-grade players a fall basketball season at County gyms around Maui.
body:
The County of Maui’s 2026 Menehune Basketball League is underway, giving sixth-, seventh- and eighth-grade players a fall basketball season at County gyms around Maui.

The Department of Parks and Recreation scheduled the league from Sept. 1 through Dec. 10. Registration was free, and the County said registered players would be placed on teams.

The program is one of the County’s recurring youth-sports offerings and provides a recreational basketball option for Maui middle-school-age players.

title: Maui golfers Austin and Lee win divisions at Maui Junior Championship
excerpt: Two Maui junior golfers finished atop their divisions at the Maui Junior Championship at Kāʻanapali Royal Golf Course. Artie Austin of Wailuku won the 9-Hole Flight, while Lakota Lee of Kīhei won the Boys 15–18 division.
body:
Two Maui junior golfers finished atop their divisions at the Maui Junior Championship at Kāʻanapali Royal Golf Course. Artie Austin of Wailuku won the 9-Hole Flight, while Lakota Lee of Kīhei won the Boys 15–18 division.

The Hawaiʻi State Junior Golf Association | First Tee – Hawaiʻi event was played Aug. 29–30 and drew 50 junior golfers from around the state. The 36-hole championship also awarded points toward the association’s Player of the Year standings and December Tour Championship.

For Maui families, the results put two local players at the top of their respective divisions in a statewide junior field on a Maui course.
